title: Verification evidence matrix and sales demo scenarios
content:
Context and purpose:
This is a working note for sales + SEs to stitch together credible evidence when pitching open models from the Redwood catalog. The goal: reduce buyer uncertainty by mapping concrete evidence types to buyer questions and a short, repeatable demo script they can run during a call. Meant to be lightweight — use as checklist before demos and for one-pagers attached to proposals.

Quick thesis:
- Buyers who prefer open models want transparency and reproducibility more than proprietary-model mystique. They need signals that the model is: licensed appropriately, benchmarked on relevant tasks, stable across versions, and safe for their domain.
- Redwood’s "verified profile" should be a noise-reduction layer: one-page collection of signal artifacts SEs can cite in <2 minutes.

Evidence types (ranked by buyer confidence impact):
1) Reproducible eval artifacts (highest impact)
   - What: test prompts, scoring scripts, sample inputs/outputs, expected metrics and seed.
   - Why buyers care: shows you ran the numbers and can be audited.
   - Quick SE line: "We ran a 100-sample prompt set (shared) and reproduced the exact F1 / ROUGE numbers — here’s the script and raw outputs."

2) Real-world reference tasks / case snippets
   - What: short before/after examples from real customers (sanitized) or realistic synthetic cases tailored to buyer domain.
   - Why: shows applicability and potential delta.
   - Quick SE line: "In a customer pilot in fintech, swapping to this variant reduced hallucinations on numeric extraction by ~35%. Example: [short snippet]."

3) License & provenance snapshot
   - What: license text, model weights origin, training-data notes (if available), any third-party attributions.
   - Why: compliance and procurement checks.
   - Quick SE line: "This model is licensed under X; we include a provenance file in the profile for procurement to review."

4) Safety/TOX scan and mitigation notes
   - What: automated toxicity scans, known failure modes, recommended guardrails (prompt templates, filters).
   - Why: risk minimization for enterprise deployments.
   - Quick SE line: "We ran toxicity scans across 5k prompts and applied a filtered prompt wrapper; here are the failure cases we observed and config we recommend."

5) Performance & cost profile at realistic latency settings
   - What: end-to-end p50/p95 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU footprint and expected cost per 1k tokens at different quantization levels.
   - Why: procurement and infra teams need to size.
   - Quick SE line: "On our medium-batch config, expect ~120ms p50 and $X per 1k tokens. We’ll attach the perf.json we publish for that variant."

6) Version lineage and stability notes
   - What: changelog for model weights/ops, behavior deltas between versions, recommended pin/rollback policies.
   - Why: customers worry about regressions.
   - Quick SE line: "This profile includes a short changelog and our recommended pin-to-hash for production to avoid surprises during rollouts."

7) Community signals and forks (lower but useful)
   - What: GitHub stars, forks, community evals, third-party fine-tunes.
   - Why: broader ecosystem corroboration.

Evidence -> buyer persona mapping (short):
- Product/PM: wants sample outputs, real-world tasks, and regression risk. Emphasize reproducible evals + changelog.
- Security/Legal: wants license + provenance + safety scans. Lead with license snapshot and mitigation checklist.
- Infrastructure: wants perf/cost + quantization notes. Provide p50/p95 and GPU footprint.
- Data/ML Engineers: want scripts, tokenization quirks, and eval harness. Share eval repo link and minimal example to run locally.

Demo scenario library (3 short, repeatable scripts)
1) "Sanity and safety minute" (2–3 min) – For early discovery calls with security/legal on the line\   - Show: license snippet, safety-scan dashboard screenshot, 3 sanitized failure cases and mitigation template.\   - Outcome: reduce procurement friction; schedule deeper security review.

2) "Task fit microbench" (5–8 min) – For PM/ML leads\   - Show: run 6 domain-specific prompts (customer-provided or template), show side-by-side with buyer’s existing baseline (if available), attach reproducible eval gist.\   - Outcome: surface whether the open model is directionally better and decide to pilot.

3) "Cost + perf sizing" (3–5 min) – For infra/ops\   - Show: p50/p95 numbers for the model variant, cost per 1M tokens at suggested batching settings, and expected GPU type. Offer a follow-up load test.\   - Outcome: get initial capacity signoff and identify Dedicated vs Hosted preference.

One-pager structure (for the verified profile) — keep to single page:
- Topline: model name + short one-line claim (what it’s good for)
- Quick signals row: license | p50 (small seeds) | safety score | stability rating
- Evidence attachments: eval gist link | perf snapshot | provenance file link | mitigation checklist
- Suggested use cases and quick example prompt + output (2 bullets)
- Recommended configuration for production (quantization, batch, routing policy)
- Known limitations and recommended guardrails

Competitive notes (unpolished):
- Major proprietary APIs lean on brand + curated finetunes; buyers assume they pay for quality and support. Our angle: transparent, auditable evidence is more persuasive for regulated customers and platform teams who need reproducibility.
- Some inference vendors provide only high-level perf numbers — this creates a gap: we can win by providing raw perf artifacts + minimal scripts that infra teams can run.
- Competitor play: "we did these evals but won’t share scripts" — call that out in SE training as a credibility lever.

Objections and suggested rebuttals (short):
- "Open models aren’t stable": Show changelog + recommended pinning; offer canary/rollback policy template.
- "We can’t trust third-party models for PII": Offer private deployment/pin + on-prem options; document data flow and no weight updates during inference.
- "We need benchmarks on our data": Offer a quick pilot template: 1-week pilot, our eval harness, 2k prompts (customer-provided or synthetic) and go/no-go metric.

Operational checklist for SEs before demo (tick-box style):
- Attach verified profile one-pager (yes/no)
- Confirm license/provenance ready (yes/no)
- Perf snapshot for the model variant (yes/no)
- Safety scan + mitigation ready (yes/no)
- Example prompts matched to buyer domain (yes/no)
- Demo notes saved to github snippet (yes/no)

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve (notes to self):
- How opinionated should the one-page score be? (numeric score vs qualitative tags). I lean toward 3 simple tags (Audit-ready | Pilot-ready | Production-ready) with short rationale.
- Do we publish the eval repo publicly or gated behind a support request? Public increases credibility but can be noisy. Possible hybrid: curated public folder + gated deeper artifacts.
- Need to standardize the perf measurement harness (sequence-length slices, batch sizes). I put an engineering request in Jira (GT-1428).

Next steps (practical):
- Draft a template one-pager and attach to 5 high-priority open-model profiles (priority: 1) Llama-variant, 2) code assistant model, 3) compact converser). Owner: Marco Li. Due: 2026-01-10 (slipped).
- Create 3 demo snippets in github repo and link in profiles. Owner: Daniel Park. Due: 2026-01-24.
- Host internal "SE rehearsal" to walk through the three demo scenarios and collect redlines. Suggested date window: Feb 1–7, 2026.

Notes to self: keep the verified profile lightweight — SEs will not read long PDFs during calls. The one-pager should be a structural elevator pitch, with links to deeper artifacts.

End of doc — this is intentionally informal. Ping me (Aisha) for follow-ups or if you want a quick working session to map this to specific models.
